posts.title: How to organise a job search: a simple 5-step system
posts.excerpt: Most job searches fail from disorganisation, not from lack of effort. Here is a simple system for tracking roles, planning your days and following up on time.
posts.seoTitle: How to Organise a Job Search: A Simple 5-Step System
posts.seoDesc: A practical system to organise your job search: track roles and companies, plan each day, and follow up on time. Includes a weekly routine and checklist.

blocks.h: A job search is a project with many small moving parts: roles you saved, applications you sent, people you need to follow up with, interviews to prepare for. Most people run it from memory and open browser tabs, and then lose good opportunities to plain disorganisation. This guide shows a simple system you can set up in an afternoon.

Effort is rarely the problem. The usual failures are quieter: you forget which version of your CV went to which company, a recruiter replies and you miss it for a week, or you apply to twenty roles in a rush and cannot say why you chose any of them.
Honest note: a better system will not fix a CV that does not match the roles you apply for. Fix the match first, then organise.

blocks.x: Step 1: Keep every role in one place

blocks.h: Pick one home for all roles and companies. A spreadsheet works. A dedicated tracker such as HV Vault does the same job with less typing, because you can save a job from a link instead of copying details by hand. What matters is that nothing lives only in your head or in an open tab.

blocks.alt: HV Vault pipeline board with wishlist, saved, preparing and applied stages
blocks.cap: Every role in one board, from wishlist to offer. HV Vault.

blocks.x: Step 2: Record the few details that matter

rows: So you can compare options fairly
So you know what each company saw
So you can follow up by name

blocks.x: Step 3: Plan the day, not just the search

blocks.h: A long to-do list of applications creates pressure without direction. Choose two or three outcomes for the day, for example: send two tailored applications, follow up with one recruiter, practise one interview answer. A one-task-at-a-time planner such as HV Reset suits this, because it keeps one task on screen with a focus timer instead of a wall of tasks.

blocks.alt: HV Reset focus timer showing one task at a time
blocks.cap: One task on screen, with a timer. HV Reset.

blocks.x: Step 4: Follow up on a schedule

blocks.h: Following up is where most candidates lose ground, because it is easy to forget and slightly uncomfortable. Set the next action date when you apply. A short, polite message after about a week is normal. If there is still no reply, one more nudge is reasonable, then move on.

blocks.alt: HV Vault action centre listing follow-ups that are due
blocks.cap: A good tracker tells you who to follow up with today. HV Vault.

items: Apply and write the follow-up date in your tracker.
Send one short message on that date.
If there is no reply, send one more a week later.
Then mark it closed and put your energy into live opportunities.

blocks.h: Spend twenty minutes once a week. Count what you sent, what got replies, and which roles are worth more time. Drop what is not working. This is also where you notice patterns, such as one type of role that keeps leading to interviews.

blocks.alt: HV Reset overview with tasks completed, time worked and score
blocks.cap: A weekly look at what you planned and what you did. HV Reset.

blocks.x: Using AI without losing your voice

blocks.h: AI tools are useful for first drafts of cover letters, for tailoring a CV summary to a job description and for practice interview questions. Treat the output as a draft. Check every fact, keep your own examples, and remove anything that does not sound like you. Recruiters read many near-identical letters, and a specific personal detail stands out.

items: Choose one place for all roles and companies
Add the five key details to every role
Pick two or three outcomes for tomorrow
Set a follow-up date on every application

blocks.h: You can run this system with a spreadsheet and a calendar. If you would rather have it ready-made, these two tools were built for exactly these steps.

items.q: How many jobs should I apply to each week?
items.a: There is no single right number. Fewer, well-matched and tailored applications usually work better than many rushed ones. Choose a number you can do properly, then adjust after your weekly review.

items.q: How soon should I follow up after applying?
items.a: About a week is a common and polite gap. Send one short message, and one more a week later if there is no reply.

items.q: What is the best way to track job applications?
items.a: Anything you will actually keep updated. A spreadsheet is fine. A dedicated tracker saves typing by letting you save roles from a link. The key is recording the next action and date for every role.

items.q: Can I use AI to write my cover letters?
items.a: Yes for first drafts and tailoring, but always check facts and add your own examples so it sounds like you.
